channel.title: Brain Waves
channel.description: Dev sessions and notes, distilled into something to listen to.
channel.itunes:author: Niall Faughnan
channel.itunes:summary: Dev sessions and notes, distilled into something to listen to.

item.title: 15. Why Your CI Deploy Chases a Commit That Never Existed: The Merge-SHA Race
item.description: A per-PR deploy hunted an image tagged with a commit that had been regenerated out from under it — a merge-SHA race. Why merge commits get a new SHA with identical parents, why the head SHA is the stable identifier, and the two-registry gotcha that made the first fix only half a fix.

item.title: 14. When 'Healthy' Lies: A Missing IAM Role, a Schedule That Ran Nothing, and an S3 Write That Wasn't Fixed
item.description: Three QA debugging stories where things looked fine until you checked the source, plus a config-registry isolation problem and a GitHub/Slack review-bot bug.

item.title: 13. The Pod Was Talking to the Wrong Database: Diagnosing Deploys by Source, Not Symptom
item.description: Two sessions on debugging failing per-PR Dagster deploys on Kubernetes: the failure taxonomy (taints, QoS, OOM-kill vs CFS throttling, rolling replacement) and the diagnose-by-source-not-symptom method behind the run-pod-vs-code-server database trap.

item.title: 12. The Deploy That Raced a Build That Hadn't Started Yet
item.description: Five since the last roundup: debugging a Kubernetes Dagster deploy (throttle vs OOM, Loki cardinality, runner cold-start), a secret sync that silently ate 24 keys, uv lockfile drift across a monorepo, browser codecs & HLS transcoding, and a competency-based interview method.

item.title: 11. The Deploy Worked — So Why Was the Build Red?
item.description: Per-PR preview-env image resolution and the deploy-vs-check distinction, self-hosted CI runner cold-starts, cross-env deploy secrets (OIDC/ESO), splitting Terraform from a monorepo, LLM context/model-internals, and a personal reminder bot — the threads since the last roundup.

item.title: 10. Four Rabbit Holes in One Day: Dependabot Lock Drift, a Phantom Image Tag, Self-Hosted Runners, and a Dead Dock
item.description: The day in four segments: Dependabot lock-file drift and how a Claude session's context window works; the three-layer per-PR image-resolution bug; ARC self-hosted runners with base+overlay and node pools; and a USB-C DisplayLink dock fix.

item.title: 9. Seven Kubernetes Lessons From One Stubborn Deploy
item.description: Seven transferable Kubernetes lessons from one afternoon of getting services deployed and healthy: a config-key mismatch that looked like a broken container, single-node vs autoscaling capacity, coordinator vs step pods, why stuck pods never auto-reap, dual-stack DNS on IPv4-only pods, requests vs limits, and OOM observability gaps.

item.title: 8. Why Your Pod Throttles at Startup: A Readiness Probe That Cost a Whole CPU
item.description: A deployment that kept failing for reasons unrelated to the code — a tour through how Kubernetes enforces CPU limits, the difference between request and limit, CFS throttling mechanics, load-aware gRPC health checks, and how a readiness probe quietly cost a whole CPU core. Transferable lessons for any containerised service.

item.title: 7. Why a Half-Idle Node Won't Schedule a Pod — Infra Lessons from a Per-PR Environment Build
item.description: Six transferable infra lessons: Kubernetes scheduling by requests (not usage), autoscaler node-pool CPU budgets, GitHub Actions trigger gotchas, a self-erasing secrets pipeline, split-horizon VPN DNS, and shared-vs-ephemeral environment design.

item.title: 6. How Dependabot Really Works in CI — Two Subsystems, a Secrets Trap, and a Lockfile Bug
item.description: Why one routine Dependabot bump sat with five failing checks, and what each taught about how Dependabot actually behaves in CI: two separate subsystems (version vs security), GitHub starving bot PRs of secrets, a path-filter gap that hides broken lockfiles, and the uv path-dependency stale-lockfile bug — plus why we accepted the manual uv lock fix over automating it.

item.title: 5. Reviewing and Fixing a Dagster-on-EKS Migration PR: Script Injection, Database Isolation, and Tests That Lie
item.description: A structured review of one large pull request — the AI-Eng half of moving Dagster onto new per-account EKS clusters — and the fixes it drove: blind-detection review, a GitHub Actions script-injection hole, the shared-DB migration-stamping incident and per-PR Neon isolation, an envsubst override trick, CI-gating false comfort, orphaned tests, and resolved-vs-fixed.

item.title: 4. Building the Per-PR Dagster Environment — From Helm Flag to Live URL
item.description: How the per-PR Dagster environment went from design to a clickable URL: Helm values layering and the condition footgun, StatefulSets and the PVC helm leaves behind, the shared ALB IngressGroup, Karpenter scale-from-zero, and the three-layer fix for CI races on destructive steps.

item.title: 3. Deploying Dagster to a New Cluster: Triggers, Accounts, and the Two-Owner Split
item.description: Moving Dagster off an old shared Kubernetes cluster onto new dedicated EKS clusters, and reshaping the CI/CD that deploys it: GitHub Actions triggers, AWS accounts and image registries, the SRE/AI-Eng ownership split, selector vs cascade deploys, YAML anchors, and an expensive env-var misconfiguration.

item.title: 2. From git push to running pods — CI/CD anatomy, and the three bugs of PR 1494
item.description: The second half of the PR 1494 story: how a git push becomes running pods, what the deploy recipe does step by step, how container images and their tags really work, and the three genuine bugs found and fixed — a verify script that always cried wolf, a stale secret address, and a merge that produced a broken config.

item.title: 1. Kubernetes, Helm, and GitOps — the foundations under your Dagster platform
item.description: The conceptual ground walked while taking ownership of the helm-user-code PR: what Kubernetes actually is, how Helm charts work, what ArgoCD does all day, and how the team's two-owner split architecture hangs together — the corrected, final understanding worth reinforcing.
